https://www.thetimes.com/culture/film/ar.title: Deep Water — Ben Affleck and Ana de Armas’s film affair
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/film/ar.text:
★★☆☆☆Much laughter, although unintentional, is likely to greet Adrian Lyne’s woozy erotic thriller Deep Water, which is based on a 1957 Patricia Highsmith novel about a couple who drive each other to murderous rage with their infidelities. Ben Affleck plays Vic Van Allen, a man so rich his house in New Orleans resembles a photo shoot from Interiors magazine. “I build web apps and publish poetry,” says Vic. “Most of the time I ride my mountain bike and hang out with my daughter.” Oh and he breeds snails. You know the sort.
He also has a beautiful wife, Melinda (Ana de Armas), who likes to get drunk at parties, cavort in the pool, sleep with handsome young men, then invite them around for supper the next day — you know, just the three of them, for a cosy tête-à-tête. “If you were married to anyone else you’d be so f***ing bored you’d kill yourself” she snarls. Affleck, unsurprisingly, looks like a man nursing a tricky molar.
I suspect he’s supposed to find all this a turn-on. Lyne is the master of the feverish erotic thriller, having made Indecent Proposal in 1993 and Fatal Attraction in 1987. This one has all their atmospherics, none of the plot and the gloopy pace of one of Vic’s snails. Has Affleck already killed one of her lovers? Does he plan to kill another? If so, could he please get on with it? With his puffy, unshaven face, hunched shoulders and air of perpetual embarrassment, Affleck mostly looks mopey as hell.
To judge from the way Lyne films de Armas — long lingering shots of her legs and ass — she’s supposed to be setting Affleck, and the film, aflame with desire, but no actress can pick pubes from her teeth and retain her dignity. Filmed while Affleck and Armas were a couple, Deep Water seems to be a misbegotten vanity project greenlit in the first flush of a celebrity couple’s hots for one another, completed just as they break up, and thereafter politely ignored by everyone involved. Affleck first did this with Jennifer Lopez — it is Gigli with a body count. TSAdrian Lyne, 115 min
Rebellion★★★★☆This inside-access documentary about the protest group Extinction Rebellion — creators of disruption as a way of demanding action on climate change — focuses on a few individuals. They include the group’s zealous co-founder, Roger Hallam, whom we see alienating his daughter, Savannah Lovelock, with his refusal to consider her views and those of other young members. Meanwhile, the lawyer Farhana Yamin, a veteran of UN meetings and other conventional forms of campaigning, wrestles with whether or not to join XR’s law-breaking protesters. Is she prepared to glue herself to a building? The film-makers could probably have done more to assess XR’s effectiveness and its future prospects. Their movie is rewarding, though, as a collection of human stories. EPIn cinemas, 15, 83min
Long Live My Happy Head★★★★☆Gordon Shaw, the subject of this documentary by Will Hewitt and Austen McCowan, is a Scottish comic-book writer and artist in his early forties who has lived for several years with a brain tumour. The film tells us that his work has given him a way of trying to cope with his condition: he has channelled his energies into an autobiographical project. Perhaps, then, the movie’s failure to give this work close attention is a weakness. But simply as a portrait of a good man going through a hellish ordeal (with the support of his boyfriend, Shawn), this is a film of great poignancy. EPIn cinemas, 15, 90min
Hive★★★★☆A based-on-a-true-story drama about women banding together to defy sexist men by running a small business, Blerta Basholli’s film would be a typical feelgood piece if it were British. Its setting, however, is a village in Kosovo, and the women — including the film’s central character (Yllka Gashi) — lost their husbands in the 1990s war. Years later, the missing men have still not been confirmed as dead, and the bereft women are expected to continue behaving as submissive wives. When they team up to produce and sell ajvar, a red-pepper condiment, the response from the village’s men is brutal. The story still has a few formulaic steps, but it’s strong and engrossing. EPIn cinemas, 15, 84min
Paris, 13th District★★★☆☆Shot in crisp black and white, the latest film from the versatile Jacques Audiard (the maker of Rust and Bone and The Sisters Brothers) is a drama about young-ish people who aren’t quite sure what they want from love, lust and life in general. A handsome, sexually confident man (Makita Samba) drifts from a fling with an equally assertive woman (Lucie Zhang) into a trickier relationship with an insecure worrier (Noémie Merlant). Social media plays its part, but the story’s flow springs mainly from face-to-face scenes. Audiard and his co-writers, Léa Mysius and Céline Sciamma, understand the way relationships can change course suddenly and without much prompting. Yet, as perceptive and realistic as the film is, it didn’t make me care what would happen to its characters. Despite their vigour, they’re faintly dull. EPIn cinemas and on Curzon Home Cinema, 18, 105min
Fresh★★★☆☆Borrowing ideas from Get Out to address male violence against women, Mimi Cave’s film stars Normal People’s Daisy Edgar-Jones as a woman trying her luck with internet dating. Just when it seems she will never find a halfway bearable man, she bumps into a potential Mr Right, a charming, self-effacing doctor (Sebastian Stan, who recently played Tommy Lee in Pam & Tommy). But it turns out he’s only interested in her body — in a horribly gruesome way. What unfolds is an effective horror thriller: it’s pacey, well visualised and not too predictable. Unlike Get Out, though, it lacks original, evocative metaphors. For all its satirical intentions, it’s basically just a meat market. EPDisney+, 114min
X★★★☆☆Ti West’s film has sex and violence pretty well covered: it’s a splatter movie in which the butchered victims are a low-budget film crew working on a porn flick. West doesn’t try to make this material any grander than it should be. Within that scope, however, he does good work. Set in rural Texas in 1979, the film has a strong flavour of that time and place, and of 1970s horror movies. The characters (played by a cast that includes Mia Goth, Martin Henderson and Jenna Ortega) have sparky conversations in the early scenes, and the eventual killings are staged with brio. Perhaps the film’s efforts to say something about desire and old age are a touch graceless, but they have definite novelty value. EPIn cinemas, 18, 106min
Europa★★★☆☆Like The Revenant and 1917, but on a much smaller budget, Haider Rashid’s thriller stays with a single character as he scrambles through dangerous terrain, never knowing what might be coming his way. Sympathetically played by the British-Libyan actor Adam Ali, he’s a young Iraqi who has made it to the Turkish-Bulgarian border and now finds himself chased through woodland by mercenaries hunting illegal migrants. Beyond pointing out that nobody deserves to be treated like this, the film’s short, rather anticlimactic story is unable to say much about immigration, so its use of that topic seems a mere piety. Still, Rashid’s film-making is impressive: the movie’s best sequences are full of tension. EPIn cinemas and on Amazon, Apple TV+, Curzon Home Cinema, Sky Store et al, 12A, 72min
Master★★☆☆☆Mariama Diallo’s film conjures up a horror-movie vibe — with possibly supernatural scares — as a way of tackling a form of real-life horror. The two lead characters are black women who encounter racism at an Ivy League university (a fictional one, but Diallo went to Yale). Jasmine (Zoe Renee) is a new student patronised and mistreated by her white peers, and Gail (Regina Hall) is a “master” — a professor in charge of a hall of residence — who begins to question her white colleagues’ smug liberal postures. The film’s satirical range is invigorating, but the ghost-story elements are finally just clutter, and the bleak ending, suggesting that people of colour will never feel at home in America’s oldest universities, seems hopelessly defeatist. EPIn cinemas and on Amazon, 15, 98min
Three Floors★☆☆☆☆Nanni Moretti has a decent track record as a writer-director — in films such The Son’s Room and Dear Diary — but his latest is exhaustingly dull. Focused on three households in a middle-class apartment block in Rome, this melodrama covers ten years in the lives of its characters, so they have plenty of time in which to do something interesting — yet they rarely manage it. The liveliest events come early on, with a married man (Riccardo Scamarcio) having sex with a flirty under-age teenager whose grandfather he suspects of child abuse. Before the story ends, however, even this tangle has been converted into the film’s standard currency: soporific conversations. EPIn cinemas, and BFI Player and Curzon Home Cinema, 18, 120min

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/tube.title: Tube protest was wrong, admits Extinction Rebellion activist
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/tube.text:
An Extinction Rebellion activist who enraged commuters by climbing on top of a Tube train admitted yesterday: “We got it wrong.”
Mark Ovland, 38, and his fellow protester James Mee, 37, unfurled a banner saying “business as usual = death” while angry passengers bombarded them with coins, coffee and sandwiches.
Mee was pulled on to the platform at Canning Town station in east London and kicked by commuters during the morning rush hour on October 17, 2019.
Edmund Blackman, prosecuting, said the pair were on top of the train for only 20 minutes but 48,000 people had their morning journeys disrupted.
After the men were given 12-month community orders, Ovland said: “We had the best of intentions but this time we got it wrong.”
Judge Silas Reid told the pair: “Each of you was part of a team under the wider Extinction Rebellion umbrella.
“This was a protest about a hugely important area. It is, though, irrelevant whether your argument is on the right side entirely or not.
“Of course, climate change is a vitally important matter for everyone to consider for the future. What you did, though, is you went too far.”
Mee, an accounts administrator from Bristol, and Ovland, a former teacher from Keinton Mandeville, Somerset, had parted company with their defence barristers after Reid ruled that there was no legal defence available to them.
A jury at Inner London crown court convicted the pair of obstructing engines or carriages on railways under the Malicious Damages Act 1861. They had denied the charge.
After handing down the verdict the jurors said in a note: “We wholeheartedly support the cause.” They said the verdict was based on the law rather than their personal feelings.
The protest was part of a two-week event when Extinction Rebellion protesters targeted DLR trains in east London stations, including Shadwell and Stratford.
The focus of the Canning Town protest was financial institutions and bankers in Canary Wharf, but the result was to prevent ordinary commuters from getting to work by train and, in some cases, losing pay.

image.caption: An Extinction Rebellion activist who held up tubes said “we got it wrong”

author: James Callery

https://www.thetimes.com/sport/football/.title: Forest Green Rovers chairman Dale Vince funded top-flight pitch invasion protests
https://www.thetimes.com/sport/football/.text:
The Forest Green Rovers chairman has revealed that he funded the environmental protests that disrupted two Premier League games last week.
Protesters bearing the slogan “Just Stop Oil” ran on to the pitches at Everton’s Goodison Park and Molineux, of Wolverhampton Wanderers, each armed with a cable tie. During Everton’s 1-0 win against Newcastle last Thursday, a man attached himself to a goalpost and had to be cut free, while an activist at Leeds United’s 3-2 victory against Wolves was apprehended before he could get that far.
Dale Vince, a green-energy industrialist who is a shareholder in the Sky Bet League Two club, told talkSPORT that he gave money to the organisation responsible for the protests, but insisted he did not know how they would use it.
“They reached out and said they wanted to start a new campaign and would you help us with a bit of cash, and I did,” the 60-year-old said. “What they didn’t say to me was that they were planning to disrupt football matches, which I find amusing. I am funding the disruption of Premier League games.
“I don’t really have a problem with what they are doing as long as they are non-violent protests. Disruption is part of protesting.”
Vince’s admission led to the suggestion that, as a club chairman, he could be charged with bringing the game into disrepute. “I’d be surprised,” he said. “If you don’t stand up for what you believe in then what’s the point in living?”

image.caption: Protesters stopped Premier League games with their protests, but Vince insists he didn’t know what the protests would be

https://www.thetimes.com/sport/football/.title: Protester has to be cut free with bolt cutters after tying himself to Everton goal
https://www.thetimes.com/sport/football/.text:
Everton’s crucial Premier League victory against Newcastle United on Thursday was held up for almost seven minutes when a protester tied himself to one of the goalposts.
The man, who has identified himself as 21-year-old student Louis McKechnie, entered the Goodison Park pitch early in the second half and attached himself to a post by wrapping what appeared to be a cable tie around his neck.
The match had to be paused while security staff attempted to remove McKechnie, who was wearing a T-shirt supporting a group called Just Stop Oil, from the pitch. The mechanical engineering student had to be cut loose with a pair of heavy duty bolt cutters.
Even then the protester would not leave the field of his own volition. He dropped to the ground and had to be carried by several members of the security team and police officers before being arrested. Another supporter was arrested after entering the pitch to confront McKechnie.
In a pre-recorded video that was posted on Just Stop Oil’s Twitter account, McKechnie explained why he had protested: “I’m about to disrupt a football match and I’m terrified, but I believe that as many people as possible need to know what a possible future holds.
“Billions of people not knowing if they should stay in their homes or if they leave where they can go as countries become too hot to live in. Mass starvation due to crop failure, it’s fighting for bread in the bakery aisle of Morrisons.
“The cost of living crisis, Covid and the war in Ukraine are showcasing this future,” he continued. I want my government to do all that they can to stop this coming true but they are expanding oil and gas, making things worse, increasing the risk.”
A spokesman for Merseyside Police said: “A man was arrested after encroaching onto the pitch during the Everton v Newcastle United Premier League fixture. At around 8.55pm it was reported that a man disrupted the match by running on to the pitch and tying himself to the goal post at the Howard Kendall Gwladys Street End.
“The suspect, a 21-year-old man, has been arrested on suspicion of pitch encroachment. He is now in police custody. The game resumed and has now concluded.
“A second man, 39, was arrested on suspicion of assault and of pitch encroachment and is also in police custody.”
Just Stop Oil were quick to claim responsibility for the stunt, issuing a statement via Facebook which read: “This evening, Louis, a 21-year-old supporter of Just Stop Oil, locked on to the goalpost at Goodison Park wearing a Just Stop Oil T-shirt, causing the referee to briefly stop play.”
The environmental group’s statement went on to criticise the government’s policy on North Sea oil.
McKechnie was previously arrested and sentenced to three months in prison for protesting with Insulate Britain. He was one of several climate activists who broke a government injunction by gluing himself to motorways.
The incident comes after an apparent attempt by the same group to disrupt Wednesday’s game between Arsenal and Liverpool but on that occasion a protester did not make it to the pitch.
